title: Non-Parametric Mutual Information Estimation with Vine Copulas
claim: A joint density factorizes into a product of simple pair terms, and the density ratio is exactly the subset of terms spanning both variable groups.
layout: 1 panel, triangular grid read top-to-bottom, colored regions with callout labels
description: A single equation, f equals a product of terms, laid out as an inverted triangular lattice. The top row holds the marginal densities f1 through f6, joined by times signs. Each lower row holds pair copulas with increasing conditioning sets: c1,2 through c5,6, then c1,3;2 through c4,6;5, down to c1,6;2,3,4,5 at the bottom tip. Three pastel shaded regions group the terms. A salmon triangle at upper left is labeled f_X and covers the terms of the first variable block. A blue triangle at upper right is labeled f_Y and covers the second block. A teal diamond in the middle is labeled f/(f_X f_Y) and covers the cross-block copulas that make up the density ratio. Thin colored leader lines connect each region to its label. The eye goes first to the colored shapes.
caption: Identifying the density ratio from a D-vine density. Functional arguments are omitted to simplify notation.
abstract: We introduce VINE: a non-parametric mutual information (MI) estimator based on simplified D-vine copulas. Approximating the joint density with a simplified D-vine allows the density ratio to simplify to a product of pair copulas, which we can estimate non-parametrically. This structural simplification yields VINE, a flexible and computationally efficient MI estimator. We compare VINE against SotA neural MI estimators on a range of datasets, both under settings where the simplified D-vine assumption holds and where it is violated, demonstrating competitive accuracy at a lower computational cost for low- to medium-dimensional datasets.
